chapter: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
title: Hawkins' return from Europe and 'Body and Soul'
summary: Thomas describes musicians dismissing Hawkins after Europe and his answer with 'Body and Soul', a solo modulating through three keys.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Now, another thing about Coleman Hawkins, when he went to Europe, he stayed about three years... When he come back to New York, everybody was saying he was a has-been. Everybody. All the musicians. "Aw, he done come back too New York, but he's been away from the States too long. He can't play." They were just saying that about him. And somehow or another... I never did check this with him either. Somehow or another, I think he got wind of it. And that's when he went and recorded "Body and Soul." Now, when "Body and Soul" was first written, nobody tried to jam "Body And Soul." They jammed all them other conventional songs. But nobody played no solo. If you played "Body and Soul" you just played the melody. And Coleman Hawkins went and recorded "Body and Soul," and that recording... What can I say about it?

It's the most... For a Jazz solo, it's the most accurate Jazz solo ever written. Because the miraculous thing he did, it changes keys three times. And he modulated into each change of key. And he almost had to have planned that solo before. Because he started out... [SINGS]...started out with the melody. That's how he started it, very melodic. And one thing, when he recorded "Body and Soul," ain't nobody said nothin' about Coleman since. Now, when Bebop come along, he played Bebop just as good as any of the Bebop guys you can name. I don't care who you name.
He surrounded himself with Don Byas and Budd Johnson.

He just played it as good as any of them. He changed his style, as I know of, three times; maybe four, because I don't know what he did before he changed to tenor. But when I checked with his mother and she said he played cello, I said to myself that's why he had that feeling for that sound. See, because the tenor is closer to cello than anything else. The only thing that's closer to cello is the baritone. But he was a genius.
